Statement by Secretary General of the National Integrity Commission Nafha Hussain:

Yes! Thank you, Honourable Chair. I am Nafha, Secretary General. I will proceed with this presentation. What we are submitting today is a presentation based on the key performance indicators given by the Majlis regarding the work carried out by the National Integrity Commission in 2025. In this presentation we have mainly highlighted the results achieved from the work carried out by the Commission in 2025 to improve the integrity of the employees of law enforcement agencies, and of the agencies, in relation to the agencies; the results achieved from the work carried out by the Commission to build public trust in law enforcement agencies; the results achieved from the work carried out by the Commission regarding establishing national-level policies to strengthen the work of law enforcement agencies; and in addition, regarding the work carried out by the Commission in enforcing the Commission's law; and then, in addition to reporting, the challenges the Commission faced, that the Commission faced in doing these things. Among the work done to strengthen the work of law enforcement agencies, we first look at how the cases submitted to the Commission regarding law enforcement agencies have been investigated. Accordingly, in 2025 a total of one hundred and ninety-six cases were submitted to the Commission concerning law enforcement agencies. Of these, one hundred and sixty cases were registered at the Commission, and full investigation of those cases began during 2025. The Commission decided on three hundred and eight cases in 2025. This includes, in addition to the one hundred and sixty cases the Commission decided to register, fifty-four cases it decided not to register, and ninety-four cases in which the Commission completed full investigation.

On average, in attending to cases the Commission, the Commission has spent eight days. Then on the Commission's own initiative twenty-three cases, twenty-three cases concerning law enforcement agencies, the Commission began investigating in 2025. Then the Commission did not hold any public hearing in 2025. In addition, I will share further details regarding these same submitted cases. In this regard I will briefly describe how the cases submitted to the Commission were submitted and the ways in which those cases were submitted to the Commission, okay. Of the cases submitted to the Commission and those it began looking into on its own initiative, 87% are cases submitted to the Commission concerning the Maldives Police Service. Then of these 10% concern the Correctional Service, and in addition 1% of cases concern Immigration. Then very few cases have been submitted to us concerning Customs. Just one case to us. Then looking at how cases were submitted to the Commission, members of the public submitted 81% of the cases submitted to the Commission. Then state institutions submitted 7% of cases to the Commission. Then 10% of the cases the Commission was looking into in 2025 are cases investigated on the Commission's own initiative. Then from employees, from employees of law enforcement agencies, approximately 0.9% of cases have been submitted concerning those agencies. Then in 2025 the Commission completed the full investigation of a total of ninety-four cases. This includes cases whose investigation the Commission began in various years. Accordingly, one case from 2019. Three cases from 2020. Two cases from 2021. Twelve cases submitted in 2022. Seven cases from 2023. Twenty cases from 2024. And in addition, I would like to point out that forty-nine cases submitted in 2025 were investigated and completed within that same year. Then within this same KPI, during 2025 we submitted two cases to the Prosecutor General's Office. Of these, 1 case was a case that was ongoing in duty prosecution at the end of 2025. Then three cases were being investigated by the Commission during this past year 2025 under a joint investigation agreement. Those 3

cases include two cases that were being investigated in a joint investigation with the Maldives Police Service, and then a case that was being investigated together with the Police Service and the ACC, by the ACC and the Commission jointly. Then here, the time we spent attending to cases has not been calculated in that way. Then as the second KPI, this concerns the things the Commission did regarding building public trust in institutions. Then the KPI. Then in the last column is the result or output achieved by the Commission based on that KPI. In 2025 the Commission did not carry out a public satisfaction survey. However, the Commission held a public awareness event, an event to raise public awareness. In addition, as part of the activities to mark Global Integrity Day, a mass lecture and a panel discussion were held in 2025. Then in 2025 two cases were submitted to the Commission by employees of law enforcement agencies. Then I would point out that those two cases were still at the investigation stage at the end of 2025. Then in addition, regarding visits to law enforcement agencies to see how work is carried out in those agencies, we have made inspection principles, guidelines. Then every inspection is carried out in accordance with a toolkit or checklist determined for carrying out that inspection. So, a specific toolkit is determined for each inspection. Then in 2025 we carried out two inspection visits. Then 3 reports have been compiled. These 3 reports include an inspection report on Malé Custody, and then an inspection report on Hinmafushi Asseyri Jail. In addition, a report compiled regarding matters noted in connection with the hunger strike at Maafushi Jail. Then in connection with the investigations conducted by the Commission in 2025, a total of twenty-six recommendations or pieces of advice have been given to law enforcement agencies. Then the Commission did not receive aid from any international organisation in 2025. However, in 2025 we signed an MOU with the UN in the Maldives, a capacity building MOU. Its work is still continuing this year. Then likewise

looking at the policies and regulations compiled, to implement national-level policies we, although we did not achieve very big results from it, we have done some work: during 2025 a great deal of work was carried out to hold an integrity symposium to discuss the things that could be improved in connection with the concerns that exist regarding law enforcement agencies. In this regard a great many administrative matters were finalised; however, due to budget constraints we have not been able to put it into practice. However, in 2025 too we gave three pieces of advice to agencies to review policies in connection with cases investigated by this Commission. And at the same time, 6 pieces of advice have been given to agencies to review regulations, the regulations made by the agencies, and to draw up new regulations. Then to increase employee awareness, three awareness sessions were held for employees of law enforcement agencies during 2025. Then among the work done to enforce the Commission's law and strengthen its administration, the Commission passed a regulation on fines in 2025. Then in addition, the Commission's law on administration has been amended. In addition, six procedures were passed in 2025 to strengthen the Commission's administration. Then in addition, internal procedures have been drawn up on how cases the Commission investigates on its own initiative will be carried out. Then the Commission did not compile in 2025 a special report as specified in Article 58 of the Commission's law. Then looking at the Commission's budget and reporting, the Commission received a budget of 16.3 million rufiyaa in 2025. Then of this, 15.84 million has been spent. Then approximately 97% of the budget was utilised during that year. Then in 2025 the Commission sent its financial report to the Auditor General's Office within the specified period. Then the Commission received an unqualified, a clean report. Then I would also point out that the annual report was published and the annual report was sent to the Majlis and to the President's Office within the period specified in that law. Then looking at the main difficulties the Commission faced in 2025, the Commission's budget ceiling is very small.

Then when the budget ceiling is set, most of the ceiling is allocated to employees and administration. Then I would point out that a very small part of the budget is there for running programmes. Then that was a very big difficulty we faced in doing additional things. Then at the same time we faced many challenges in retaining technical employees. That is because to this day the Commission remains an institution not harmonised under the pay harmonisation under the pay framework newly introduced by the government, newly introduced by the state. So, I would point out that due to that challenge many of our technical employees left throughout the year. Then we have many difficulties in obtaining the training opportunities employees need to develop capacity, technical, especially training opportunities such as investigation. And I would point out that even with the opportunities that come, due to our small number of employees, sending employees to those opportunities has become a very big difficulty for the Commission. Then in addition, in investigating cases, in investigating these cases, we also face challenges due to not getting the cooperation of complainants and agencies. Then I would point out that those difficulties also exist with the technical capacity of employees in investigating certain kinds of criminal cases. Then at the same time I would point out that the Commission also has difficulties in obtaining evidence, in obtaining evidence in connection with cases. Then that is, these are the things pointed out as the main difficulties faced by the Commission. Then, just two minutes, okay. At the end of 2025 the Commission had thirty-two staff. Then the Commission's work is organised under three divisions. Then just to share a brief summary of the work done by the Commission in 2025. Thank you.

Statement by Member for Baarah constituency Ibrahim Shujau:

Thank you, okay. The National Integrity Commission, as you would know, is a commission whose mandate a great many citizens, and a great many, especially when we were in the opposition, a commission on which many citizens' eyes are very much fixed, okay. So, my question is, when the SG summarised just now, no direct percentage was given of how many cases you looked into on your own initiative. So, how many cases have you looked into on your own initiative, okay. Then shall I say it all together? It would probably be easier for the SG to answer them all together, right? Then how many cases are submitted by private parties, okay. Then once a case is looked into and completed, is there a procedure by which you inform that party how the case was concluded, okay. That is the second question. The third thing is, I believe the role of the National Integrity Commission needs to broaden a little. I believe there needs to be a mechanism by which the hard work you are doing can be brought to the public frequently. Otherwise what happens is, I truly believe, the Commission members and administrative staff, you very much, even when I came to this committee what was in my mind was that the most cases would be submitted regarding police matters. Especially because the police work to maintain peace and security. Because they are the parties that have to face citizens the most. However, the Commission's mandate, previously there was the Police Integrity Commission. The story now is that those commissions have merged and the National Integrity Commission has been formed. So, we request, then, that you consider this matter. Earlier I asked some questions. Now what I am saying is a request. I would very much like you to consider providing the public with information about the work done by the National Integrity Commission. Then in providing information to the public, you may say, for example, we publish on the website. Beyond that, I believe the work of this commission perhaps needs to be thought about broadly. That is, since the Integrity Commission is the party that assesses how transparently uniformed bodies or institutions carry out their legal mandate, and with how much independence, you

the matter of providing information to the public, like twice a month, or at least once a month, or at least once every two months, you giving that update through the press is something I believe in my heart would greatly build citizens' trust in the Commission, which is why I just mentioned that, okay. Thank you.

Statement by Vice President of the National Integrity Commission Fathimath Shareef:

Fathimath Shareef, Vice President of the Commission. What the member actually said, as I understood it, is why, why cases have been increasing more recently. Previously, in reality, the National Integrity Commission was a very hidden place. To a great many people, and still to very many people, what they know of is a Police Integrity Commission. The National Integrity Commission; many people do not know that it is a body formed by merging two bodies, the Police Integrity Commission and the Customs Integrity Commission, or what it does. Then however, as Member Insha said, when this year began, we new members joined as last year was ending. Then when this year began we drew up a media strategy, and then I think the Commission gave information to the media for the first time. Sessions giving information to TV and radio too will have been held this year. So, the more transparent it becomes, the more cases also increase. Likewise we also have a very large backlog in our hands. We are also carrying out work to clear that backlog, giving it special priority. However, the bit I want to point out is that the number of our investigators, okay, is nine this year, now. That is the number of employees we have been given. However, when this year began there were four investigators. So, that is a very big challenge for moving cases forward at the speed we want. Then I think the more cases are completed, the more the public's trust in us improves, and so cases will increase. I think that is the reason. Thank you.

Statement by Secretary General of the Anti-Corruption Commission Fathimath Nilfa:

Yes! Assalaamu alaikum. In this annual report presentation, the presentation will proceed based on the KPIs we have received from this side. Looking at the number of complaints submitted to the Commission, a total of one thousand and twenty-nine complaints were submitted to the Commission. Of the complaints submitted, five hundred and two cases were registered. The number of complaints not registered is five hundred and twenty-seven. Within this I would like to point out that two cases were submitted for case review again. Looking at the number of cases registered, a total of five hundred and thirty-three cases have been registered. In addition, including cases the Commission looks into on its own initiative and split cases, a total of five hundred and thirty-three cases were registered at the Commission in 2025, and split cases are cases where, from within a case the Commission is investigating, further cases or a specific party are involved and each part requires a separate investigation, and in such situations it is decided to register each of them as a separate case and look into it. Number of cases concluded; the number of cases registered is five hundred and thirty-three. A total of three hundred and fifty-one cases were concluded in 2025 at the investigation stage and the preliminary stage. Looking at the time taken to conclude cases, six years are spent at the preliminary investigation stage. This is actually, 0.6 years are spent. That is, the period for concluding a case is determined as the time spent between when the case is assigned to an investigation officer and when all stages are completed. Taking into account the extent of resources the Commission has for investigating cases and all these matters, every year work is planned by dividing the work into 4 quarters and prioritising cases under the priority system established at the Commission. Accordingly, A, B, C, D, these 4 priorities, A, B, C, D, are a standard used to assess the weight of a case, including the scale of work that must be done in connection with the case, and its difficulty. Then among these, A category cases are the heaviest cases. And D category includes small cases. Looking at duty prosecution and cases sent for prosecution, last year the Commission, together with the PG Office, a total of thirteen

cases, entirely new duty prosecution has been started. In addition, the Commission has decided on thirteen cases requesting that they be submitted for prosecution under Sharia. And of these thirteen cases, eight cases have been accepted by the PG Office. In 2025 the PG Office sent back a total of seven cases. And one hundred and nine cases have also been discussed with the PG Office. According to the Commission's statistics, at the duty prosecution stage a case takes on average four hundred and twelve days. When 2025 began there were ninety-six cases at the duty prosecution stage. And when the year ended there were a total of one hundred and seven cases. Looking at concluded cases, in 2025 the Commission concluded a total of one hundred and ninety-seven cases. Of these, one hundred and forty-nine cases are cases decided at the preliminary stage as not constituting a corruption offence. At the investigation stage, thirty-two cases were decided as not constituting an act of corruption because sufficient evidence and proof were not obtained. Thirteen cases were decided to be sent to the Prosecutor General's Office requesting prosecution. And in addition, three cases were also filed because the investigation could not proceed. Looking at the details of notices issued for rectification, a total of twenty-seven notices were sent. If we go to its breakdown, it includes eight notices relating to money to be recovered for the state, and nineteen notices instructing rectification. Looking at the follow-up of notices and the extent of their implementation, in order to check the extent to which state institutions have acted on notices the Commission issued to them in past years after investigating cases, a total of one hundred and forty-five follow-ups were made in 2025. Of the notices followed up, 17 notices have been implemented by those institutions. We received information that work has begun to implement the matters in forty notices. And the institutions have also informed the Commission that, for various reasons, work has not begun to implement the matters in twenty-six notices. In addition, I would also point out that at the end of 2025 the Commission had not received implementation updates on a total of sixty-two notices. Looking at the details of money notified for recovery to the state, from 2009 up to now in 2025, as money lost from the state through ACC investigations, various institutions will have been notified that one

billion six hundred and seven million six hundred and thirty-two thousand nine hundred and seventy-nine rufiyaa three laari must be recovered. Then, if the total amount of money due to the state from cases concluded by the Commission is divided over 17 years, the Commission has notified for recovery to the state ninety-four million five hundred and sixty-eight thousand eighty-four rufiyaa four laari per year, and if looked at per month, seven million eight hundred and eighty thousand six hundred and seventy-three rufiyaa sixty-seven laari. Therefore, by these statistics, for every one rufiyaa spent from the state budget on running the ACC over the past 17 years, the Commission has notified the relevant institutions to recover at least two rufiyaa eighty-five laari for the state. Going to the details of money recovered for the state, institutions have informed the Commission that of the money notified to state institutions for recovery up to 2025, a total of one hundred and seven million six thousand eight hundred and twenty-seven rufiyaa has been recovered to the state's finances. Of this, two hundred and forty-four thousand eighty-eight rufiyaa ten laari is money recovered for the state in 2025. Then I would also like to point out that recovering money due to the state is not among the responsibilities placed on the Commission by law. Looking at training programmes employees took part in, a total of thirty-four participants took part in eighteen training programmes held abroad. Forty-nine participants took part in training programmes held in the Maldives by other institutions, in total eighteen training programmes. In twelve training programmes arranged by the Commission for employees, a total of four hundred and twenty participants will have taken part. Then 66% of employees completed 10 hours of training for continuing professional development in 2025. Looking at studies, in 2025 this Commission carried out a total of two studies. Those are two social audits as social audits, and the guideline on how to act in situations of conflict of interest. Looking at social audit reports, two reports. These are a HA. Hoarafushi hospital project carried out from 3 July to 7 July. And a Sh. Funadhoo school fifteen-classroom project carried out from 30 September to 4 October. In addition, the guideline on how to act in situations of conflict of interest was launched on 9

December 2025. Looking at highlights, an international forum was held under the theme "Combating Corruption and Strengthening Integrity in the Tourism Sector". With the assistance of the European Union, the project "Accountability in Integrity Matters" has begun with UNDP as an implementing partner. And in addition, an agreement has also been signed to obtain vehicles needed by this Commission under grant aid from the Government of Japan's Economic and Social Development Programme. We have divided the challenges into these three parts. I will touch on each part separately. Accordingly, staff shortage: response to advertisements to recruit skilled people in the anti-corruption field has now decreased greatly. As a result, 50% of posts have had to be advertised repeatedly, and because of all this, administration has been greatly delayed. Compared with other institutions, salaries and benefits are low, and since no high-risk allowance at all is received, very big challenges have also arisen in retaining technical employees. In addition, I would also point out on this occasion that with the staff turnover rate at 23%, many experienced employees have been lost and the institution has faced very big challenges. In addition, going to the space constraint, because there is no office building dedicated to the Commission, very big difficulties arise in ensuring the safety and security of members and employees as well as people attending investigations and trainings. Our Commission has to be run in a house where ordinary people live. Therefore, many challenges also arise in ensuring the security of sensitive data kept at the Commission and these matters. Because there is no space at the Commission at this time, it is not even possible to set up the work stations needed for additional employees to be hired. I would point out that this is also a very big obstacle to increasing the number of the Commission's employees and to recruiting people to the extent needed. In addition, the stores in use at the Commission, the rooms where stock is kept, are also now completely full. I would also point out on this occasion that at this time there is no space at all to keep additional documents and office equipment as well as various facilities. Then looking at the lack of financial independence and budget constraints, in accordance with the internationally accepted "Jakarta Statement of

Principles for Anti-Corruption Agencies", in order to provide the opportunity to carry out the Commission's duties most fully, determining the budget in a way that ensures financial independence is absolutely necessary. In some situations, receiving approval for expenditure is greatly delayed. Within this there are a great many administrative procedures of various kinds, and because of the many procedures, the things planned cannot be implemented on time. In some situations, I would point out, I would like to point out that in 2025, due to budget constraints, some special training programmes planned to increase employees' capability could not be carried out. Thank you.

The question I want to put is, then the challenges are understood by us. Then I will say that we will do the work we are able to do on that matter in cooperation. Then with initiative a great deal of work can be done. Then the question that comes to my mind is, given the way things are organised in the Maldives now, perhaps the Anti-Corruption Commission will also be an institution that faces a great many, the biggest challenges. Criticism too will be aimed most at that one commission. In that, my question is, now your report states that 412 days are spent in duty prosecution. What is the reason that has to be so? That is one thing. Then the other thing is, as I too personally believe, the most criticism will always come, and the most criticism will be of politicians. That is not a problem. They should be criticised too. It is a responsibility of politicians to be cleared of the criticism made of them and to prove themselves as people of integrity. For example, regarding allegations made against politicians and cases looked into, I believe it is also very important that there be a mechanism by which those matters can be disclosed to citizens after the Anti-Corruption Commission has finished looking into them. And beyond politicians too. Then this is a question I want to ask, as noted from the report. Then I personally believe that your results, given the resources you have and the difficulty, are good. However, what I want to clarify as a first question is the reason so many days are spent in this prosecution.

Statement by President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Adam Shamil:
Yes! Thank you, Honourable Member. First I would very much like to thank...

Statement by the Chair:
Stating your name.

Statement by President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Adam Shamil:
I am Shamil, okay, President of the Commission. My sincere apologies! First of all, on behalf of the Commission, I would like to thank you very much for the sentiments you expressed. The view you noted regarding the Commission's budget to strengthen the Commission's affairs is, I think, a view that also aligns with international best practices. Then the Honourable Member asked about the reason 412 days are spent in duty prosecution. In that, duty prosecution has been structured in different ways at different times. Then in some situations we act on a duty in line with the advice the PG gives us. The meaning of duty prosecution, if we look at the ways we have practised it, is that in some situations, in some cases, we submit to duty prosecution right from when the case begins. And sometimes we submit once a certain level of sufficient evidence and proof for the case is obtained. And some cases we submit when they are completed. So, when those three types of cases are averaged together, it comes to 412 days. Then looking at the number of our cases, and looking at the documents involved, our cases will be cases involving a very large number of documents. That is because financial investigations are investigations based very heavily on documents, which is why that happens. So, there will be a very large number of documents. So, a great deal of time will be spent taking those materials to the PG Office and in the consultation meetings held with the officials of that field there; a great deal of time will go into studying them in light of the matters I noted earlier. So, I consider that one reason. Then another reason I consider is that, even for lawyers, this field is a very different field. This involves documents of the kind that include a great many financial documents. So, with only an education in the legal field it will be very difficult to enter into the study of this. So, that is something that will take a great deal of time. There will be cases involving very large financial analysis. And there are small ones too.

And very different types of financial analysis are also involved. There will be net worth analyses. There will be analyses connected to people's lifestyles. And we are also talking about other types of financial, very technical documentation. We too employ specialists in that field for that. So, within prosecution too, when experience is gained over many days, I believe this will change greatly. And the PG, very recently, at PGO 2.0 too, it was noted at that session, we cited as an example that the paper submitted is something that takes a great deal of time to study. They are introducing a system for it. So, here I believe we will be able to reduce these 412 days with the coming technological advancement. And also through strengthening the relationship between institutions. That, in total for me; if another person has something further to point out, it would be good if they pointed it out for me.

Statement by the Chair:
Yes! If there is nothing further from the members, yes! I give the floor to the Honourable Member for Dhidhdhoo constituency Abdul Latheef Mohamed.

Statement by Member for Dhidhdhoo constituency Abdul Latheef Mohamed:
Thank you, Honourable Chair. And thank you, President, Vice President, members, administrative staff. Before my first question I also want to clarify two or three things. You, when I looked at the report just now, what I note very much is the problem of an office for administrative work and the problem of the budget, and in addition the difficulties, the challenges in doing various things. Have you sent this to the parties concerned with this matter? What I mean is, did you also send these issues to the President's Office, the Finance Ministry and the secretariat of this Majlis? Did you send that these matters are dragging on like this, or that these cases are not being looked into because of such and such happening? Then my biggest

question is, what the general public complain about most is the issue of cases submitted to you not being looked into with independence. What the general public complain about most is the issue of those cases being delayed. The general public ask about you dragging on for many days without giving any answer on cases. Whether on the island, whether in the atoll, what the general public say in various meetings is that the responsibilities entrusted to you, the work entrusted to you, are not being carried out as adequately as they should. What is the answer you have to give to that? What answer would you give for it not being carried out? Then I see very often, especially since we are now on the same side as the government. While we are, from the other side approximately very many, by the other side I mean, especially from the MDP side, I see very many cases going in. On TV, in various news, at their various forums, I see them talking at their meetings. That because they are not given an answer, and this, and stories of you not meeting them even when meetings have been arranged with them, I see complaints being made like this from that side. The general public see these things. So, what is the answer you have to give to that.

Statement by the Chair:
Yes! Please proceed!

Statement by President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Adam Shamil:
Yes! Thank you, Honourable Member. I am the President of the Commission, Shamil. Yes! I believe the Honourable Member has asked very important questions. Among them I will try to respond to the first question. That is the question asked whether the difficulties we have in the three main areas have been shared with the relevant parties. Yes! We have repeatedly, on various occasions, brought this to the attention of those important institutions in great detail, okay. So, the Ministry of Finance in particular will know the difficulties we have. The difficulties our employees have,

the difficulties relating to our salaries, the National Pay Commission will know. Just as they were moving forward with harmonisation, we will have met them repeatedly and submitted our difficulties in great detail. And I remember there will also be a detailed report of about eighty pages at the NPC. Regarding the challenges we have, and also regarding the matters we have noted in the technical document in which the NPC has now determined the salary structure it uses. So, we have told those parties about those matters in great detail. Then the Honourable Member asked what I believe is a very important question. He noted the concern among the general public in three main areas. First, regarding our independence. I think that regarding our independence, it is very often expressed in a very political way. But we are not a commission over which there is political influence to any extent. We are acting in accordance with the standards set for us by laws, regulations and procedures, in light of the standards the criminal justice system has set for us to follow. So, we have no doubt about that. We are operating with independence. Then in connection with those matters there are always views expressed out of political concern, or in light of beliefs they politically hold. We also respect that. But the answer we have to give to that is that we run this institution, and all our affairs, especially investigations, by ensuring the rights set out in the criminal justice system. And also by establishing a system by which those rights can be ensured. You will note that none of our cases are necessarily carried forward by setting an order of priority we choose. It is something that runs by giving marks and weighting. In our investigations, taking into account the political sensitivity at a given time, we also slow things down. And we also speed things up. Especially regarding elections, we also make decisions in order to avoid things that might make people think there could be some kind of influence on us

decisions. So, in that way the Commission is being run, I believe, in light of the law, the Constitution and the regulations set for us as an independent institution. Then the concern regarding our cases being delayed. I truly believe that is an existing concern. In investigating our cases, you will note that even the first stage takes 0.6 years. Meaning approximately two-thirds of a year or 6 months. But our categories "A" and "B" will take a little less than that. Meaning we have greatly sped up the time for cases we investigate with highest priority over the period that has passed. However, the "C" and "D" included in our categories are something that takes a fair number of days. So, on average at this stage approximately half, six months, half a year passes in this. So, we accept that this is a real concern. For the purpose of improving that, we will have established some systems within the Commission. In that regard, we have established a special system since last year to conclude long-pending cases.

And to speed up cases submitted to us, we have brought a big change to decide on small cases based on the type of case submitted. That is, we have completely changed the way our investigations were previously structured, and we have now established a system by which investigations can be carried out one after another for the purpose of speeding up investigations. Within that system a special committee has also been formed to look at cases that have existed since earlier, and that committee's work is now proceeding at a very high speed. If my information is not wrong, we have now exceeded one thousand in the number we have concluded in it. So, I note that this is a very good achievement. Then when we took over this work, we are talking about a very large number of cases that had come repeatedly on various occasions, from 2008 up to us. So, to strengthen the Commission's registration, we have again brought a very big change some months ago. In light of that, cases submitted to the Commission, only after being looked at more fully

we have changed it so that otherwise they cannot be registered at the Commission. That is the work we are doing today to resolve the concern the Honourable Member of the People's [Majlis] just noted, which we accept. Then I believe the point noted regarding not giving answers. I think that is a concern that arises perhaps as a result of some matters not being told, from some direction, to the extent we can generally tell citizens. The reason is that through the system we have now established at the Commission, automatically for anyone, if someone submits a case to the Commission with their name and phone number, automatically when a case is registered that person will receive a message. And after that, when the investigation begins they will receive a message. And every time the investigation stage changes they will receive a message. So, I can say with 100% certainty that if anyone comes with their name noted, with a phone number to contact that person, they will not go without an answer. But in cases submitted to the Commission by a party without stating a name, there is no way for us to answer that person. In that situation, however the case proceeds, since it is a case submitted in a way that does not reveal who it is, there is no way for us to answer that party, so that is not something we can do to that extent. Then the last thing the Honourable Member noted is the story that we do not answer cases submitted by the MDP. I believe that is not something that could happen in any way. As the Commission's system stands, if any party submits a name to the Commission specifying which party it is, with a name, after we register the case, everyone will receive an answer with a reference number to contact in connection with the case. Whether it is 2025. Whether it is 2024, 2023, it is something we have consistently implemented. So, it is certain that we would not fail to respond to a case submitted by the MDP. Thank you.

Statement by Member for Dhidhdhoo constituency Abdul Latheef Mohamed:

Thank you, Honourable Chair. And I have two more questions. Under the Maldives' political system today, parties are formed and it is set up for them to govern. Then also the message parties give the public has become a very important message. So, explaining your work to party leaders or to parties, or the way your work is planned, have you met any party, or, having met parties, under the current system, things the citizens accept, what citizens most do is what the parties say. They listen too, the ordinary members of parties believe what the party leaders say. So, do you work by meeting party leaders, or by meeting parties, to tell them how your work is being carried out, that it is happening this way? Or is it planned that way to any extent in your work.

Statement by Vice President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Abdulla Nashid:
I am Abdulla Nashid, okay, Vice President of the Commission. In answer to the Honourable Member's question, I have to say that previously and up to now, no activity of meeting parties to give information on how our work is planned has yet been carried out. However, sometimes political parties, depending on the political scene at a given time, do request to meet us. When they request, we do meet them without regard to any particular party. However, in our strategic plan now drawn up for the coming 3 years, we have a very big activity to carry out together with parties. As we believe, many acts of grand corruption originate through political activities. Or there is a political party, party system in the system of governance. So, closing the doors open to corruption in the funding of political activities, the funding of campaigns, and in the governance system of political parties is one of our goals for the coming three years. And especially what we aim for is, there is a presidential election two and a half years from now. And whether that work can be completed before the election, we

are working very hard. So, going forward there is work planned that we will carry out together with parties. Thank you.

Statement by Member for Dhidhdhoo constituency Abdul Latheef Mohamed:
Thank you. I will ask one more question, okay. Then in very many offices one person has been in one post for a great many days; that is not a matter that concerns you. However, because of that person, he does not go on leave, or does not go for treatment, for many years, five or six years he stays because of some benefit he gets. The biggest part of it is that, as I said, he has very large powers in that office. Procuring things for the office, and giving the office's projects to parties. Then what I mean is that he stays, remains in that post, without taking even leave, without taking even family leave, because of the size of the benefit he gets. In cases you note in that way, will you have done any kind of work to submit to the relevant parties to change that or to bring a good reform to it? Or have such cases come to you? Thank you.

Statement by President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Adam Shamil:
Yes! Thank you, Honourable Member. Then even while asking the question, you noted that you accept there is also something that does not directly relate to us. Then I believe taking leave and things of that kind are not matters within our direct mandate that we would otherwise look into. But, for example, a case where a person stays in a post without taking even leave, for a particular purpose, noted in that way and such a case submitted, I cannot note one in light of the information available to me. But we could look, by going to the office, whether cases of that type have been submitted in a way we can separately identify. Then if there are such, we could prepare it as the answer to the Honourable Member's question and share it with this committee. But so far, in that

way, in light of the information available to us, we do not have information sufficient to answer on the spot. Thank you very much.

Statement by the Chair:
Yes! I give the floor to the Honourable Member for South Fuvahmulah constituency Ibrahim Hussain.

Statement by Member for South Fuvahmulah constituency Ibrahim Hussain:
Yes! Thank you, Honourable Chair. I too thank you very much for submitting your 2025 report just now and for coming here. And at the same time I would note that a great many matters have been pointed out in your report, and a very large amount of money, from 2009 to 2025, had to be recovered and has not been received. And that you now have no role in recovering this money. That after you notify that it be recovered, your role ends at that point. However, we are talking about 1.6 billion rufiyaa, a very large amount of money not received, and when so many days have passed, and the cases that have been submitted even now, the cases submitted even now, do you have any kind of target, after a case is submitted, a date by which it will be completed, counting from the day the case is submitted? A date by which it will be decided? Then the other question is, you said just now that you are planning a very big thing within three years. My question is, when room opens up for corruption, the very first thing that comes even in our religion is awareness that paves the way to stop it before it is done. I cannot at all see now the Anti-Corruption Commission making the citizens of the Maldives aware, okay, running any programme to make the citizens of the Maldives aware. Any work being done to stop things that pave the way to corruption before they take hold. So, I think these are things we need to think about. After doing the work needed to stop it before it is done, corruption is committed. After it is committed, a great many

days in it, and later the person forgets about it altogether. Then especially the disrepute put on those governing in the Maldives or on political figures, okay. Even regarding parties that do not commit corruption at all, when the opposition or whoever wants to destroy that person's reputation, we see the scene of them putting whatever amount they want on that person's head and destroying that person. Do you have, for these parties, regarding parties who spread information in that way; that too, putting disrepute on someone's head, everything, when that person is destroyed, that person also has reputation and honour. In doing that, do you have any plan among the things planned going forward, when such parties put disrepute on someone's head, unproven disrepute. When it is done in the same way in something not even proven, when a case is submitted, such big cases, especially regarding those governing. When disrepute is put on the head of a leader, can that work be done by giving it special priority so that the general public get the answer to those cases as quickly as possible? Just now you spoke about staff difficulties, and about employees not being retained at the Commission now because salaries are low, and about approximately 23% leaving. We are talking about a very large number here. When responsible, technical, studied, educationally qualified people are needed to do work at a place like the Anti-Corruption Commission, such people leaving this job seems to me a very big loss for the Maldivian people. So, to control this, to retain such technical people at this Commission or to keep them in employment, is there any work at all being done by the Commission together with the state, together with the government, to give such parties the good benefits they need and in a way that their salaries can also be increased; is there any such plan going forward? Then the other question is, do you believe the Commission's work is being carried out in the most complete way? Thank you very much.

Statement by the Chair:

Yes! Please proceed!

Statement by President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Adam Shamil:
Thank you, Honourable Member. The first question asked concerned our figures. These figures, very large figures, have to be recovered for the state. We have no legal role, nor any power, regarding recovering those amounts, for example going to a court or taking action against those parties in clearly specified terms. There is Article 27 of the Commission's law. But that article, as it currently stands, is not in a way that fits this era most fully for us; I am talking about a 2008 law. So, we will also have submitted amendments to that. Then regarding a date by which the Commission's cases will be decided, I believe it is a very important question. We recently, in the change brought to the regulation I referred to earlier, it is now written for us in clear terms that for every case submitted to the Commission, when the investigation begins from the point the case is submitted, a date by which that case will be decided must be set. We are now carrying out the work needed to prepare the place for that and the work of making procedures. We are at its final stage. Once this procedure is followed and this work begins, I believe every case at the Commission will have been given a date. A date by which it will be decided will be set. So, I note that as a very important change we can bring. Then the Honourable Member noted an important thing that we very often forget in general, that is the work of prevention. We always focus very much on enforcing the law, on the enforcement part. But I too believe prevention is the area in which work now needs to be strengthened, with the highest priority given to it. Then but even I did not see in today's presentation a figure for our prevention activities carried out. That may perhaps be because it is not included in these key performance indicators given to us, given by the Majlis

for us, for the purpose of doing it as early as possible. But we will share with this honourable committee the awareness figures and everything carried out by us during the past year too. We can run them, okay. Even now, giving special attention, we will have done work in 2025 too regarding school children, parents, universities and Maldivian companies, together with the CMDA and likewise with the PCB. And no training programme for directors under the CMDA will go without including our programme. No CSDA [unclear] training programme for newly recruited employees will go without including us. Then for the programmes run for citizens in general, we have to go to the islands to run them. But we have very big difficulties with that. But the programme we run called social audit is a programme run together with the general public and associations and NGOs. Because the details of that programme were not given that much, I noted this because I note there may perhaps be difficulties for the Honourable Members in knowing about it. So, we can run it that way. We will give the details of its figures to the honourable committee. Then the Honourable Member also asked a very important question for us. That is, cases with no specific basis at all are sometimes submitted to the Commission, with the case lodged for the purpose of showing it is a real case. When 2/2000 (Law on Prevention and Prohibition of Corruption) existed, the concept or notion the Honourable Member noted was written directly, specifically, in clear terms, in black and white, in that law. But when that law was abolished, with the 4th amendment to the Penal Code, and that law ceased to exist, the notion you just noted is not a notion that came into the Penal Code. So, within the system we now follow, there is nothing specifically written for us, within our powers and responsibilities, on how to act if a case is submitted to us for the purpose of specifically bringing down a person's standing. But in that way, within the legal powers we now have, for example, many things are also happening directly to bring down our own standing. So, there is a system in law in the Maldives, various ways of looking into and taking action in that field on things happening in that way. Media,

if it is media, there are things that happen that way in the media field. And in other fields too, there are systems in other places by which things coming to be determined in that way can be looked into. But I will note that within us, at this moment, that system is not directly in place. Then in cases submitted to us in that way, especially political, those at the top, those in high posts, not only political. I think for example whether it is the judiciary or other fields, whether regarding those persons or in other ways, a strategy that we will use within the Commission in the Commission's actions has now been drawn up for us with the assistance of the EU. It is at its final stage. So, we have established a communication strategy for the Commission. I would also point out that it is something the Commission has never had before, made to good international standards. When it starts being followed, Honourable Member, I will answer linking it also to the question asked earlier by the Honourable Member for Baarah constituency. He asked then about disclosing the extent to which the cases we decide become known to the public. Together with the question the Honourable Member just asked, when we start following this strategy, we will have received a strategy prepared to a good standard for informing citizens generally of the things we decide and the ways we act, and it has reached the point where it can be followed. Then it was noted that the 23% of our employees leaving is now there. This issue is at a very worrying level. Very many of our employees are now in this honourable Majlis too. Leaving our places to come and work here. I believe they come because there are good benefits of various other kinds here. But the biggest challenge we faced in not being able to retain them in the past days is the challenge with our investigators' salaries. Looking at our salary in 2014, the salary now set is 466 rufiyaa, a small amount at its lowest grade. 2014, Honourable Member. So, we have a great concern. We are trying to resolve this together with the relevant parties,

working on it. Our hope is that a solution to this is found very soon and this is fully settled. At that point I believe very many people will come back to the Commission and join our team again. That is because very often their concern is not related to the field. It is regarding the benefits they receive and various matters. So, when those matters are settled and the path is further opened for us too to give them training and do more things, I believe that is a very big advancement we could achieve. And I want to point out as one last thing, very briefly, in our training programmes, as you saw, when 34 people were trained abroad too in 2025, we ran those training programmes spending a very small amount from the state budget. Meaning we obtained opportunities, together with various other institutions, from foreign countries, for example countries like Saudi Arabia, India or Malaysia, so as not to burden the state budget. So, if we receive more assistance in that area, I believe we will achieve more success in training our employees further through the assistance programmes we obtain with more countries.

Statement by Vice President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Abdulla Nashid:
I am Abdulla Nashid, okay. Wanting to add something to the President's remarks. As the MP noted, prevention, the work of protecting, stopping corruption; when one says stopping, culturally too what we have come to accept is generally awareness programmes. Then the Secretary General will have the data on the awareness programmes. However, we are now changing our thinking on this. We have been running awareness programmes alone since 2008. Has there been a change? We note that there is not a very big impact in this. People know how it happens. Citizens become aware. However, how much

force does this exert on stopping corruption. In answer to that question we can say it does not exert very much force. So, our direction now is, as also noted earlier, to identify how acts of corruption happen, in which places, identify these parts, and address these parts. So, in our three-year plan too, as I noted earlier, one thing is political parties and campaign financing. We will address this area, God willing. Then another thing identified is the SOEs. State-owned enterprises are the area where acts of corruption are submitted to us in the largest number, and among the public too, I think all citizens would accept that the most acts of corruption happen within those places, within that sector, so we will also address that within the coming three years. And we have already begun work. We are already carrying out work together with the PCB. So, we believe that if systematic matters of this kind are addressed, we will achieve a very big advancement in matters of stopping corruption, okay. Thank you.

Statement by Member for South Fuvahmulah constituency Ibrahim Hussain:
Now in corruption, we would know that very big legal measures can be taken against those who commit corruption, right. That is in the law. What comes to my mind is that you go to the SOEs themselves as a session, on what is set out in the law, the things that legally follow if something paves the way to corruption or if corruption takes hold or if corruption is committed, okay. That such and such measures can legally be taken; I think those things are often not known even to the people who do, who end up doing these things, okay. Not knowing, not knowing what is being done, they get drawn into it, often. Then so, very much as you just said, especially within the SOEs, we will see that in the government that ended in 2023 there was a case of many billions of rufiyaa in Fenaka alone, okay.

Fenaka alone. RDC's treasury has been lost many times, okay. To this day no solution to this issue is being found for us, okay. In any case it is the people's money, okay. The people's money. To the people this money; the people now cannot trust, in actual reality. It is now reaching the point where no institution can be trusted. If the money cannot be recovered for the people, it is being proven that such big corruption has been committed. It is being seen on social media. But after investigating this, as long as this money does not reach the people, it becomes like something that never happened, okay. So, to gain the people's trust, okay, to gain the people's trust, do you believe this Commission must be run more robustly than before? And in a way with greater transparency to the people about these matters, what things you are able to do for the people, which cases we have completed, recovered; the people expect you to run that Commission structured in a way that you can be a little transparent so that all these things can be done, okay. The people expect it. I just want to ask how you have planned to begin those things.

Statement by President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Adam Shamil:
Yes! Thank you, Honourable Member. I believe, as I indicated in my earlier answer, the communication strategy we have now obtained through this work done with the assistance of the EU together with UNDP, when we start following it, that will change greatly. How we will publicly disclose information in connection with cases submitted to us and the work we do, and the ways information must be disclosed at set intervals and so on, have now been drawn up to its technical standard. So, I think we are at the point where we can start following it very soon. So, a very big change that will come with it, for me; that is our plan, Honourable Member. Then, as you noted, the question asked then regarding the Commission's administration. We too accept that there are things we need to improve beyond the present. That is why we are

identifying, through the projects with important partners like the EU, the things we need to improve and running that as a project. We are running that project with very large assistance from the EU. So, a great deal of work is under way through it at this moment. To speed up our investigations, we are running that Sentinel Three Years project, in other words, within our 3-year period, digitalising things, automated digitalisation, work on AI incorporation, even at this moment. So, we have a very good team in our hands at this moment. With that team's work, the ground has now been laid for a great deal of the Commission's work. Then in the coming days we will be able to reach really good results. For example, regarding the notices we issue too, going forward the path has now opened for us to do that on a digitalised platform. Very soon, so that it is publicly visible to the public, as the Honourable Member just noted, it is a further project to increase the transparency of the work we do. With that we have reached the point where to which place we issue notices, when they were issued, which party acted on them and to what extent, is public, and the Honourable Members too can look at any time if they wish. So, every one of these, in light of the experience I have now gained, involves a great many administrative matters. A great many approvals must be obtained. For example, to establish a forensic service, with the government taking the initiative, at the Commission, as a work of the Honourable President, work is also under way to establish a complex and serious fraud office. A great deal of work is under way. But in each of these we have a great many difficulties. But even so, in light of the work we are able to do, I believe the work we are now doing is very important work for us. In light of this work our forensic service is being established. With the forensic service, for investigating corruption in the Maldives, serious

and complex investigations, with the standard being drawn up and the capability we are establishing, we will gain the path to quickly carry out the many matters citizens are concerned about. Then today, if my information is not wrong, this honourable Majlis has reached a very big advancement for asset recovery work as well. And just today, by coincidence, when I came to attend this committee, the honourable Majlis has also decided to take part in the Saudi Arabia, "Makkah Al-Mukarramah" OIC convention. So, I believe very big advancements will continue to be gained with such matters of the state. That is the OIC, the body involving the most countries in international governance after the UN. So, with the assistance from one country to another through what happens there, I believe further advancements will be gained with our taking part in it. So, we have a specifically set plan to strengthen and improve the Commission's administration. Work is under way under that plan. But I too believe our investigations still need to be sped up. Need to be strengthened. And things need to be increased to the extent that our investigations need to be visible to the public. We are doing that.

Statement by the Chair:
Yes! I would like to conclude; is there anything further to point out from the ACC side before concluding?

Statement by President of the Anti-Corruption Commission Adam Shamil:
Thank you, Honourable Chair. What I most want to point out is that the amounts determined to be recovered for the state in the past years in the Maldives after the Anti-Corruption Commission was formed are not something that can be let go, and that the work of recovering them for the state must be done by the relevant institutions. We now, civil asset

recovery, we will have a project in our hands in which we have obtained all the details of what has happened up to this point. We are now starting that work. In light of it, a system is being established by which, within a digitalised platform as I noted earlier, it can be monitored which amounts must be recovered and brought back from each institution and how much of that has been recovered. Along with that, we will start work together with institutions, together with the most important relevant institutions. And recovering those amounts for the state is, as I believe, something that will achieve one of the most important, most fundamental purposes of the existence of the Anti-Corruption Commission. Our greatest wish is to receive from state institutions the assistance and cooperation we need to do that. And I also assure this honourable committee that we always work, in accordance with the standards set for us in light of the laws, without leaning to any party, without depending on any party, to carry out the responsibility entrusted to us as well as possible, to the extent of our capability. Thank you.

Statement by the Chair:
I give the floor to the Honourable Member for Baarah constituency Ibrahim Shujau.

Statement by Member for Baarah constituency Ibrahim Shujau:
Wanting to share a small experience, okay. As I believe, reducing the role of humans in matters is a very good measure that could be taken to stop corruption, as the committee too believes, and the Commission too. The reason I say this is that with the changes brought under the policy of digitalising some institutions now, when services previously done by some institutions are digitalised, what happens is that the doors to doing wrong things are closed, okay. When I looked into such a matter reported to me by someone in the meantime, the President just now too, the ACC President

noted, I believe the advice you give too, and the work done especially using AI and technology, stops it. So, as I believe, if the Commission works well, if you get your resources and can work, especially, as the Vice President of the Commission noted just now, the SOEs, these issues that have existed since the start, since this system was formed, I think we will have to resolve going forward in order for us to bring this country to a different direction. I believe the results of work done now will begin to be seen within a year or two of starting the work. So, I believe establishing a centralised procurement system and pushing for this to be done through a digital system is a very important thing. Then I believe, as the ACC President noted, even when we worked on the Finance Committee back then, the biggest challenge the ACC had was not retaining employees. That is, employees you have trained are being lost from your hands because they do not get good pay. Then it is a very big concern in actual reality. That is why we too are pushing very hard to obtain financial independence for the Anti-Corruption Commission. At the same time, the ACC President has just answered many of the questions I actually wanted to ask. Along with that too, what happens is that since the Maldives is a small country and everyone is very much digital, or especially socialised through the phone, I would point out that, for the things that are said, to ensure the integrity of politicians and others prominent in other matters against allegations made against them, concluding cases quickly is in actual reality a very important thing. Even while noting that, we note it while accepting the challenges you have. So, as I believe, the corruption problems in the Maldives can only be solved when a mechanism comes by which all institutions involved in this matter can work together. While the ACC works, if the stage at which the Prosecutor General prosecutes the work the ACC does is delayed, the purpose we want is not achieved. Then if the work the Prosecutor General's Office must do, the work done in connection with a corruption case, is not sped up within the judiciary, that purpose

is not achieved. A verdict is being delivered this year in a case the Anti-Corruption Commission looked into in approximately 2012. This is not how it should be in this system. That means it is being delayed from some direction. With the ACC having been quick, the PG having been quick, the court is being slow. So, as I believe, if the work done in parallel between those three institutions is strengthened, I believe in my heart it will improve. So, we in the committee will also note your concerns. We will also do the work we can do, and I also say that we will do it. Thank you very much.

Statement by the Chair:

Yes! God willing, very soon we will hold a visit to the ACC on behalf of the committee. Then by the time we go on that visit, please prepare the matters you have noted as a paper! For example, that this is the main reason employees do not stay there, very briefly. Then the budget constraints and that. Then coming up is the budget debate. This session will end after the budget is passed. So, when it comes to our committee's attention, God willing, we too will bring those matters to the attention of the Finance Committee. Then last year a great many attendance complaints came from some institutions. But not one complaint about the ACC has come to us so far; by attendance I mean complaints about members' attendance. Some people come when they want. But no such complaint about the ACC has come, either from employees or from the general public. So, that is something we note with gratitude. Then I sincerely apologise because today's meeting was a little later than we expected. We came here having given you a time, and at 11 o'clock, as we were about to start the NIC meeting, we learned that a vote had to be taken. Then because of that, that half hour got pushed back. So, once again I sincerely thank all the ACC members, the SG, and the other employees too. I hope that the work we all do together will, God willing, be good work that everyone accepts

and welcomes. And I hope that, God willing, we will meet you very soon on our visit. Thank you very much, everyone. At this point our meeting has concluded.
